stories.headline: 5.9 earthquake rattles Japan: 23 injured, trains disrupted; no tsunami threat
stories.title: 5.9 earthquake rattles Japan: 23 injured, trains disrupted; no tsunami threat
stories.summary: In the early hours of Sunday, eastern Japan experienced a moderate earthquake, with injuries reported for over twenty individuals, primarily minor. The strong tremors caused significant disruptions in transportation services, including train delays across the region. A water pipe burst was noted in Tokyo, alongside power outages affecting numerous homes. Fortunately, no tsunami threat emerged, and nuclear facilities remained secure.

stories.headline: Ukraine-Russia War
stories.title: Ukraine-Russia War
stories.summary: On August 20, Russia launched one of its heaviest aerial attacks on Kyiv, killing at least 16 people and injuring more than 40. Residential areas, a school and a children’s medical facility were among those hit. Ukraine’s air defences intercepted many cruise missiles and drones, but its shortage of Patriot interceptors left it vulnerable to ballistic missiles. At almost the same time, Ukraine has been escalating its own attacks against Russia. Hundreds of drones have been sent deep into Russian territory, striking military and energy infrastructure. In recent weeks, Russian oil facilities, ports, logistics centres and industrial sites have come under attack. A recent Ukrainian strike involving nearly 800 drones was one of the largest of the war. It is a conflict that has become normalised. And that may be more dangerous. There is something uncomfortable about the way the Russia-Ukraine war has slipped down the world’s news agenda. The guns have not fallen silent. The casualties have not stopped. The missiles and drones are flying almost every night. Yet, compared with the first two years of the Russia-Ukraine conflict, the war now receives far less attention. The fear is that the conflict may be entering one of its most dangerous phases when the world’s attention is elsewhere. The Iran-US war has presently consumed headlines, diplomatic bandwidth and military resources. Washington is preoccupied with the West Asia, European governments are dealing with their own wider consequences of the conflict, and media are dominated by images of missiles over Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Israel. Ukraine, once the defining geopolitical crisis in Europe, has become almost a background story. When Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, the expectation in Moscow was apparently that Kyiv would fall quickly. Instead, Ukrainian resistance halted the Russian advances. The war then settled into the kind of conflict where small territorial gains measured in kilometres, sometimes metres. The war-front now stretches for roughly 1,200 kilometres. Russia continues to grind forward in parts of the east, while Ukraine tries to make the cost of every Russian advance high-priced. This is not a frozen war. It is an active war of attrition. And attrition has a cruel arithmetic. A few hundred metres gained may mean hundreds of lives lost. A destroyed refinery may cost millions of dollars but does not necessarily change the military balance. A missile attack can kill civilians without producing any meaningful territorial change. That is precisely why the outside world is losing interest. The West Asia has suddenly become strategically more important to Washington. American air-defence systems, interceptors, aircraft and other military resources are under pressure. The Ukraine conflict, that required a continuing supply of ammunition, air-defence missiles and financial assistance is feeling the pressure. Ukraine is facing a shortage of Patriot interceptors at a time when Russia is increasing its missile and drone attacks. The problem is not simply financial. The United States and its allies have their own stocks to replenish, and West Asia has created additional demands. For Kyiv, this is a frightening development. Russia exploits a divided Western strategic focus. The Kremlin has repeatedly demonstrated its willingness to wait, absorb losses and continue fighting while hoping that political fatigue will eventually weaken Western support for Ukraine. Millions of Ukrainians have been displaced. Thousands of civilians have been killed. Yet casualty figures have become abstractions. The news of thousands killed no longer sends the shock it once did. Hundreds of drones sound almost like a normal, routine game. Perhaps the biggest danger of the new normal in prolonged war is suffering being measured by numbers and no human or emotional values. The latest Russian attack on Kyiv should have made major international news. Instead, it competed for attention with Iran, US diplomacy, oil prices and the wider West Asia crisis. Hardly, there is any global attention. Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones and long-range weapons. Unable to match Russia tank-for-tank, missile-for-missile or soldier-for-soldier, it has adopted an asymmetric strategy. Ukrainian forces have targeted Russian oil refineries, energy facilities, ports and military sites deep inside Russia. Such attacks can hurt Russia economically and militarily, but they are inviting stronger retaliation. Moscow has responded with intensified attacks on Ukrainian cities and infrastructure. Another major change is taking place within Ukrainian society. After the invasion, hundreds of thousands volunteered, driven by a strong feeling that the country was fighting for its survival. Four years later, that spirit has weakened. Asking people to join a war with no clear end is very different from asking them to defend their country in the first weeks of an invasion. The controversy over forced mobilisation, known as “busification”, reflects this growing frustration. There have been allegations of men being forcibly taken to recruitment centres, abuse by recruitment officers and corruption over medical exemptions. Human rights groups have raised concerns about unlawful detention and mistreatment. The stories of soldiers returning from the front and confronting angry civilians are particularly revealing. One Ukrainian veteran quoted in recent reporting asked, in effect, what they had fought for if soldiers could themselves be attacked by citizens. The political debate is becoming more complicated. Ukraine remains under martial law, which prevents normal elections. That was understandable when Russian forces were approaching Kyiv. But the longer the war continues, the more difficult it becomes to sustain a democratic system indefinitely without a clear political timetable. The emergence of criticism from former officials and political figures is therefore significant. It does reveal war fatigue and demand for political leadership change. And Russia is waiting for precisely this. Moscow does not necessarily need to conquer all of Ukraine. It may only need to outlast Ukraine’s political patience and its allies’ financial patience. Western governments have continued to support Ukraine financially. The European Union recently announced that Rs 1.4 billion from interest generated by frozen Russian central bank assets would be directed towards supporting Ukraine. This is important, but it also illustrates the central paradox of the conflict. The West has imposed sanctions on Russia, yet the Russian economy has adapted. Moscow has redirected trade, found alternative markets and continued financing a war economy. Sanctions have imposed costs. They have not forced submission or defeat. The lesson is not that sanctions are useless. It is that sanctions alone cannot end a war when the adversary is prepared to absorb economic and human costs. Military pressure, diplomacy, economic pressure and political incentives have to work together. Perhaps the most depressing part of the present situation is that diplomacy has almost vanished from public discussion. There have been American efforts to mediate. There have been direct contacts and proposals. But there has been no breakthrough. Russia continues to insist that any settlement must reflect what it calls the “realities on the ground”, while Ukraine refuses to accept territorial concessions imposed by force. Moscow has also continued to reject proposals that merely freeze the existing front. The Iran war has made the diplomatic vacuum worse. And so the war continues almost by inertia. That is perhaps the most dangerous phase of any conflict, when nobody believes victory is close, nobody can agree on peace, and everyone becomes accustomed to the killing. The Iran war is undoubtedly a major strategic crisis. But the existence of another war cannot make Russia- Ukraine tragedy less consequential. In fact, the two conflicts are increasingly connected through military resources, energy markets, American strategy and the calculations of Russia and Iran. For India, there is an additional reason to pay attention. New Delhi has maintained relationships with both Moscow and Kyiv and has consistently called for dialogue and diplomacy. Moscow continues to be India’s reliable and tested partner. India’s position has always been that lasting peace cannot come through military means alone. The longer the war continues, the stronger the case becomes for a serious diplomatic effort that recognises Ukraine’s sovereignty and security concerns while also addressing Moscow’s concern as well as the larger European security architecture. The world cannot afford to wait for a battlefield collapse before returning to diplomacy. Russia-Ukraine conflict may no longer dominate the front pages. But people are still dying there. Cities are still being bombed. Soldiers are still being buried. Families are still living without electricity, security and certainty about tomorrow. A war should not become less tragic because another war has become more dramatic. The greatest danger now is not only that Ukraine may lose territory. It is that the world may slowly lose its sense of urgency and eventually accept a permanent war of attrition as the new normal. And it would be a failure of diplomacy. Surinder Singh Oberoi, National Editor Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: 25 years of non stop journey
stories.title: 25 years of non stop journey
stories.summary: On Sunday, 26th August 2001, at around 7:45 pm, when the signature tune of “Radio Kashmir Pesh Hai – JK Bank Diary” went on air for the first time, no one imagined that this 15-minute programme would still be on air, without a single break, 25 years later. This Sunday, JK Bank Diary completes its Silver Jubilee. 25 years. 1300+ episodes. 325+ hours of broadcast. Networked on 8 stations of Radio Kashmir – Srinagar, Jammu, Leh, Kargil, Poonch, Rajouri, Bhaderwah and Kathua. In the history of All India Radio, no commercial sponsored programme of 15 minutes weekly has ever had such an uninterrupted, revenue-generating run. It is, perhaps, a national broadcasting record. And it all began mid-air. Love at first hear: Bangalore to Srinagar, 23rd June 2000 The story is now folklore in broadcasting circles. On 23rd June 2000, this writer was waiting for a flight from Bangalore to Srinagar. In the lounge, I spotted a tall, graceful personality – Mr. M.Y. Khan, Chairman, J&K Bank. We boarded together and destiny gave us seats together. For three hours, I poured my heart out. “Khan Sahab, Radio Kashmir talks about Chinar, Kehwa, Saffron, Pashmina – everything beautiful. But we never talk about the empty pocket of our farmer. We never tell our artisan that his shawl has a price in Paris. Our own bank – J&K Bank – is our pride, but for a common man in Kupwara, it still looks like a locked government office. Why doesn’t J&K Bank itself tell its people what the Bank is and what does the Bank have for them?” Mr. Khan did not just listen. He heard it. For the entire flight, we discussed only this. It was, as i later called it, love at first hear. As we landed at Srinagar, he held my hand and said: “Rafeeq, come to Zam Zam, my office. The idea born in the air must get wings on the ground.” A week later, in his chamber at ZamZam House, Corporate Headquarters, the idea got wings. And in that same chamber, another history was born – the immortal tagline that became the voice of Kashmir: “JAMMU & KASHMIR BANK – BADHIYA, BE-NAZEER BANK” It was not written by an ad agency. It was an emotion born in that room. Then it is history. Birth at Tagore Hall: 24th August 2001 For one full year, the format was worked out with my friends Qaiser Mirza and Air Voice Advertising. The brief was clear: No jargon. No preaching. Just 15 minutes of soulful conversation in Kashmiri, Urdu, Dogri and Gojri. Mr. M.Y. Khan showed rare vision. He approved it not as advertisement expense, but as Zimmedari – Corporate Social Responsibility, long before the term became fashionable. The programme was formally launched on 24th August 2001 at Tagore Hall, Srinagar. The evening was doubly special – it also had a Talha-Majboor comedy show. The Chief Guest was the then Chief Minister Dr. Farooq Abdullah, who blessed it saying, “This is the best use of Radio.” Next day, 26th August 2001, Sunday, the first episode went on air. I was sitting near my old Philips radio set at home, holding my breath. When I heard the words, my eyes were moist. A new chapter in Indian commercial broadcasting had begun. A team that never let it die A programme does not run for 25 years on one man’s idea. It runs on a team’s ishq. At Radio Kashmir, the early pillars were G.N. Rattanpuri, Late Bashir Shah, Late Ashraf Bhat, and Anjali Sharma at Jammu. In marketing and production – Shakeel Bakshi, Zahoor Zahid, Meraj Din Ahmad, G.R. Akhoon, Wajih Siraj, Bashir Buch, Late Mansoor Ansari and Late Mustafa Ansari. Engineers – Late Jamil Baksh, M.Y. Shah, A.K. Handoo, Irshad, Mushtaq – supervised by Ayaz Malik, produced it free of cost in our studios. Initially, the Bank hired our studio. When I suggested to Khan Sahab that the Bank should have its own media team, he did it. He created it. And Sajad Bazaz, a brilliant Mass Communication pass-out, carried it brilliantly for years. The first trusted voices were Zahoor Zahid and Ms. Roohi Sultana. Later, fresh voices gave it new colour. 25 years ago the Bank was banking upon us for recording and editing, now it is fully self-sufficient with its own infrastructure. That journey itself is commendable. Through floods of 2014, earthquake of 2005, curfews, snowstorms, and COVID-19 – when everything stopped, Radio did not stop. Tapes were recorded in makeshift rooms, but “tape ready hai, Sir” – that call never missed. What did 15 minutes do? The format was simple but powerful: Aghaaz_ – an opening note, Bank Aapke Ghar Par – scheme explained in mother tongue, Sawal-Jawab – listeners’ letters, and Kamyabi Ki Kahani – the soul, a real success story. We never sold loans. We removed fear. We told people – Bank se daro mat, Bank tumhara hai. Long before Delhi invented the slogan of Financial Inclusion, J&K Bank and Radio Kashmir were practicing it. The impact? Go to Shopian – a farmer knows pledge finance. Go to Zaina Kadal – a weaver knows export credit. Go to Rajouri – a woman knows how to form a Self Help Group. That awareness was created in those 15 minutes. So much so that for three consecutive years, JK Bank Diary figured in the Balance Sheet and Annual Report presented to the Board and published in The Quest– the Bank’s journal – with a noting: “Because of this programme, our credits have increased manifold and advances have touched skies.” Khan Sahab, I only conceived it, you delivered it on the ground. Whose jubilee is it? If someone asks me today what is my biggest contribution in 40 years of broadcasting, I will say – 15 minutes every week for 25 years. But this Silver Jubilee is not mine. It belongs to the listeners of Radio Kashmir – that farmer from Anantnag who wrote, “Loan ko Kashmiri mein samjhao,” that mother from Bhaderwah who asked, “Meri beti doctor banna chahti hai?” It belongs to the clients of J&K Bank – that boy from Baramulla who took Rs. 50,000 and became an exporter, that widow from Kishtwar who now employs 10 women, that student from Kupwara who is now a doctor in Delhi. And it belongs to the J&K Bank family – from M.Y. Khan Sahab, my co-passenger who gave it wings mid-air, to every CMD thereafter, every Executive President, every Branch Manager and clerk who said, “This programme must go on.” Today, as a professional listener, I can say with pride – JK Bank Diary still holds priority among listeners for knowledge, information and entertainment. It is still a high-ranking programme of Radio Kashmir. An archive request My only request on this Silver Jubilee is – let these 1300 scripts be archived. They are not just scripts. They are the economic history of 25 years of Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh, told by its own people, in their own voice. And perhaps, the officers of All India Radio, the Bank and record keepers should note – JK Bank Diary is perhaps the only programme in Indian broadcasting which holds a record as a commercial and revenue-generating creative for 25 years uninterrupted. If otherwise, please correct me. It started on 26.08.2001. It is still on. It is not a programme. It is a Rishta. A 25-year-old relationship between a Bank and its people, tuned in every week on radio waves. Shukriya listeners. Shukriya J&K Bank family. Shukriya M.Y. Khan Sahab. Dr. Rafeeq Masoodi IBS (Rtd), Former ADG, Doordarshan

stories.headline: Fight for reservation, constitutional rights still on: Aga Ruhullah
stories.title: Fight for reservation, constitutional rights still on: Aga Ruhullah
stories.summary: National Conference Member of Parliament Syed Aga Ruhullah Mehdi on Saturday said his fight for reservation and the restoration of constitutional rights and protections for Jammu and Kashmir was far from over. He, however, launched a sharp attack on the government over the reported hike in electricity tariffs. Talking to reporters on the sidelines of a book launch ceremony here, Ruhullah said the “biggest fight” was for the constitutional rights and protections of J&K, asserting that he would continue to pursue the mandate given to him by the people. “The fight for reservation is still going on. I am fighting for reservation. The biggest fight is for the constitutional rights and protections of our state. That fight is still going on,” he said. Ruhullah said he had tweeted a few days ago informing his students that he was still with them and “on the streets”. “Last time, they needed me. I was ahead of them. I will continue to be ahead of them. But they need to be brave,” he added. The Srinagar MP said he had not abandoned the fight for reservation, recalling that a sub-committee was formed after a protest outside the Chief Minister’s residence, but its recommendations had not yielded results. “After our protest outside CM residence, a sub-committee was formed and the results did not come. Even after that, we tried to protest again last year,” Ruhullah said. Ruhullah, however, said he had come to realise that an even bigger battle facing politics was the erosion of political principles and values. “The political character is missing. There is no character in our politics,” he said. He further accused the J&K National Conference of making promises and commitments before elections and subsequently abandoning them. He said his political fight was aimed at bringing “principles, values and character” back into public life and urged the younger generation to take the political system into its hands. “I don’t have any personal desire. I want this fight to be fought by the new generation of Kashmir,” Ruhullah said, adding that journalists, sportspersons, artists, doctors and educationists must contribute to bringing “character, conviction and values” into politics. On the reservation issue, the MP said he had not abandoned students who had been demanding their rights. He, however, claimed that fear had been created among them following alleged raids on their homes and hostels. He said he was ready to stand with students if they came out peacefully and democratically to protest. “I did not stop the fight for reservation,” he said. Ruhullah further said he would try to ensure that students did not face punitive action for peacefully raising their demands. He also said that if there were consequences, he would face them along with the students. Ruhullah rejected the suggestion that student protests were a “flop show” because of low participation, saying the circumstances surrounding the protests needed to be understood. The MP also defended his recent remarks about the possibility of resigning, saying he had not issued a deadline for anyone to step down but had set a timeline for himself to take his advocacy for J&K’s constitutional rights to another stage. “I got the people’s mandate and worked inside and outside Parliament, including through lobbying with opposition parties, to build support for restoration of constitutional rights and protections,” he said. Ruhullah said his advocacy had yielded results, claiming that opposition parties had joined the debate over J&K’s constitutional status and statehood. He said he needed “a couple of parliamentary sessions” and “a couple of months” to take his campaign forward before taking a decision on his political future. Taking aim at his own party leadership, Ruhullah said the party had diluted the issues on which it sought votes. He alleged that the demand for restoration of Article 370 and constitutional guarantees had gradually been reduced to statehood and other issues. “They have weakened the fight themselves. Diluted it,” he said. He also hit out at the government over the reported increase in electricity tariffs, pointing to the election promise of providing 200 units of free electricity. “Instead of giving 200 units free, nearly seven percent increase has been made in tariff,” Ruhullah said. He recalled Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s earlier remarks about throwing electricity meters into the river, saying the promise of free power had not materialised even after two years. On remarks by the US ambassador regarding Kashmir, Ruhullah said he did not seek legitimacy from the American administration on the issue. “If I get legitimacy from the American ambassador, I want to throw that legitimacy into the sea,” he said. He said Kashmir’s political status was an internal matter and had nothing to do with the United States. He also questioned the US position on conflicts in Palestine, Iran, Yemen and Lebanon and asked whether the Indian government had raised these issues with the American administration. “This is our internal matter. It has nothing to do with America,” Ruhullah said. Referring to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s meeting with the US Ambassador, Ruhullah questioned whether the Chief Minister had raised concerns over the killings in Palestine or submitted a protest note to at least register his protest before the ambassador. He asked whether such issues had been raised during the meeting, saying that if Kashmir’s political issues were an internal matter, the same principle should also apply when discussing international issues with foreign representatives.

stories.headline: Imran Khan, Pakistan Army at fresh crossroads as political crisis deepens
stories.title: Imran Khan, Pakistan Army at fresh crossroads as political crisis deepens
stories.summary: The political confrontation between jailed Pakistan Tehreek- e- Insaf (PTI) founder and former prime minister Imran Khan and Pakistan’s powerful military establishment appears to have entered another critical phase, with both sides facing off over his possible release and medical treatment. According to political experts, developments being discussed in Pakistan, Army Chief and Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir has made it clear that any arrangement concerning Imran Khan, whether related to his release from prison or his transfer to a private hospital, would have to be negotiated with the military establishment rather than secured solely through an order of the Supreme Court. The issue has further widened the longstanding rift between Imran Khan and the Pakistani military. Since entering national politics, the former cricketer turned politician has repeatedly found himself at odds with successive army chiefs and senior military officers. Imran Khan’s most complicated relationship with the military establishment has involved three generals: former Army Chief General Qamar Javed Bajwa, former ISI chief Lieutenant General Faiz Hameed and current Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir. After becoming prime minister, Imran Khan appointed Faiz Hameed as Director General of the Inter-Services Intelligence (ISI). Hameed subsequently became politically close to Khan. At the time, Hameed was relatively junior in the army hierarchy but was seen as having ambitions to become army chief after Bajwa’s retirement. Bajwa was eventually given a three-year extension. Political observers at the time speculated that Hameed expected several senior officers to retire during the extension period, potentially improving his chances of becoming army chief. Relations between Imran Khan, Bajwa and Hameed, however, deteriorated. Bajwa, despite his earlier association with Hameed, ultimately backed changes in the ISI leadership. Hameed was removed as ISI chief and transferred as Corps Commander to Peshawar, while Lieutenant General Nadeem Ahmed Anjum was appointed as the new ISI chief. The relationship between Imran Khan and Asim Munir had already become strained. Munir had served as DG ISI under Bajwa in 2018 but was removed from the post after around eight months. Khan was reportedly suspicious of Munir over allegations concerning the leaking of private information relating to his wife, Bushra Bibi. The political confrontation subsequently intensified and culminated in the removal of Imran Khan’s government in April 2022 through a vote of no confidence and Shehbaz Sharif subsequently became prime minister. Munir was appointed army chief later in 2022. His rise to the top military position effectively ended Faiz Hameed’s prospects of becoming army chief. Hameed later resigned from the military and was eventually court-martialled and sentenced to 14 years in prison in a case involving allegations against him. The current confrontation comes at a time when Pakistan is facing multiple political and institutional crises. One major issue is a proposal to reorganise Pakistan’s existing four provinces into 33 administrative units. The proposal has been politically contentious, with opposition and reservations reportedly emerging within both the Pakistan Muslim League (Nawaz) and the Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP). Supporters of the proposal argue that creating smaller administrative units would improve governance and ensure that development funds allocated by Islamabad reach communities at the grassroots level. However, the proposal would require broad parliamentary support and constitutional amendments. Without the backing of major political parties, including PML N, PPP and PTI, any such constitutional package would face serious difficulties in Parliament. The disagreement has also exposed tensions between the military establishment and the country’s major political parties. The military leadership is believed to be seeking political space for a possible accommodation with PTI, while the party’s principal demand remains the release of Imran Khan. This has brought the issue of Imran Khan’s imprisonment and medical treatment to the centre of the political negotiations. Imran Khan’s camp has maintained that he should either be released through judicial proceedings or shifted to a private hospital on the basis of the Supreme Court’s directions, without any political deal with the military establishment. The Supreme Court had issued directions concerning Khan’s medical treatment and access to his family. The subsequent decision to conduct his medical examination at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad, rather than shift him to a private facility, Shafa International Hospital has added another layer to the confrontation. The political situation has meanwhile become more complicated following the announcement of a September 27 protest and proposed long march by the PTI-led government in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. At the same time, opposition parties in the National Assembly are moving towards greater coordination over Imran Khan’s imprisonment, his medical treatment and what they describe as non-compliance with Supreme Court orders. Jamiat Ulema e Islam chief Maulana Fazlur Rehman has also begun consultations with PTI and other opposition parties on the possibility of broader political coordination. If the PPP were to join a broader opposition front, the political arithmetic in Islamabad could change dramatically. A united opposition could potentially seek a vote of no confidence against the Shehbaz Sharif government, creating a situation similar to the one that brought down Imran Khan’s government in 2022. Pakistan therefore appears to be heading towards another period of intense political uncertainty, with the military establishment, the ruling coalition, PTI and other opposition parties increasingly locked in competing strategies. The coming weeks could prove crucial for Imran Khan’s political future, the survival of the Shehbaz Sharif government and the balance of power between Pakistan’s elected institutions, the judiciary and the military establishment. Any direct confrontation between the Supreme Court and the government over compliance with judicial orders could further deepen the constitutional crisis and potentially trigger demands for a change of government or fresh elections. Pakistani political experts believe Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his Pakistan Muslim League Nawaz are likely to remain aligned with Army Chief and Field Marshal General Syed Asim Munir, arguing that Pakistan’s political history has repeatedly demonstrated the decisive influence of the military establishment over the country’s political system. According to political observers, Nawaz Sharif is aware of the consequences of confronting the military establishment. His political experience, particularly the events surrounding the Kargil conflict and the subsequent military takeover, remains a significant factor in determining his approach towards the army leadership. Observers believe that if the current political confrontation escalates further, Pakistan could once again face a situation in which the military assumes a more direct role in governance, a possibility that remains a major concern for the political leadership as well as the public. The stability of the Shehbaz Sharif government could also become increasingly vulnerable if the Pakistan Peoples Party withdraws its support from the ruling coalition. If the PPP pulls out of the coalition, the PML N would lose its current majority position within the government alliance and would face serious difficulty in sustaining the government without support from other parties. The National Assembly of Pakistan has 336 seats. The ruling coalition currently holds around 243 seats, while the opposition and aligned groups have 89 seats, with the remaining seats comprising independents and vacant positions. The government side includes 132 seats held by the Pakistan Muslim League Nawaz, 74 by the Pakistan Peoples Party, 22 by the Muttahida Qaumi Movement Pakistan, four by the Pakistan Muslim League Q, four by the Istehkam e Pakistan Party, one by the Pakistan Muslim League Zia, one by the Balochistan Awami Party, one by the National Party and four government-aligned independents. On the opposition side, 75 seats are held by independents and PTI-backed members. The Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam Fazl has 10 seats, while the Sunni Ittehad Council, Majlis Wahdat e Muslimeen and Pashtunkhwa Milli Awami Party have one seat each. Political analysts say the numbers underline the importance of the PPP’s support for the Shehbaz Sharif government. Any withdrawal by the PPP could dramatically alter the balance of power in the National Assembly and force the PML (N) to seek support from other political groups to remain in office. The situation has become particularly sensitive amid growing tensions between the military establishment, the ruling coalition and the opposition led by Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf. Political observers believe that the PML (N) is unlikely to risk a direct confrontation with the army leadership, given Nawaz Sharif’s previous experience of being removed from power and arrested following the military takeover under General Pervez Musharraf. With political alliances under strain and the opposition preparing for further protests, the coming weeks could determine whether the Shehbaz Sharif government survives the growing pressure or Pakistan enters another period of political instability. (The Author is a Former Bureau Chief Aaj Tak TV, Jammu)

stories.headline: MHA panel formed to draft final agreement on Darjeeling hill issue: MP Raju Bista
stories.title: MHA panel formed to draft final agreement on Darjeeling hill issue: MP Raju Bista
stories.summary: The Centre has constituted a committee to draft the final agreement on the Gorkha issue, BJP MP Raju Bista said on Saturday, after a key meeting between Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Gorkha leaders and the West Bengal government. The meeting aimed to find a roadmap for a “permanent political solution” to the long-standing issues of the hill people. The meeting, held at a hotel in Sukna in the Darjeeling foothills on the third and final day of Shah’s north Bengal visit, was attended by Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari and leaders of various political parties of the hills and other stakeholders of the region. “A committee under the Ministry of Home Affairs has been formed under the leadership of interlocutor Pankaj Kumar Singh. It will work to finalise the drafting of today’s agreement,” Bista said. In October, 2025, the MHA appointed retired IPS officer and former deputy national security advisor Pankaj Kumar Singh as the official government interlocutor for the issue. His role focuses on leading political dialogue and addressing long-standing demands of the Gorkha community. Bista, the Darjeeling MP, said that Saturday’s meeting was held on a historic day since it coincided with the date of signing of the Gorkha accord in 1988. The accord, signed between the Centre, the West Bengal government and the Gorkha National Liberation Front (GNLF), had led to the creation of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council (DGHC) following a violent agitation for a separate state of Gorkhaland. “The history of struggle of the hill communities spans over four decades during which the previous Left and TMC government trampled over the aspirations of the hill people. The sacrifice made by our people involves nearly 2,000 people who were martyred, over 5,000 people displaced and women tortured and raped,” he alleged. Bista said that while representatives of the various communities put forth their concerns and expectations at the meeting, Adhikari also spoke on how he intends to address the issues of the hill people. “After hearing out all stakeholders, Shah summed up the meeting by elucidating how a permanent solution to the issue would be reached in the days ahead,” the MP said. The meeting was expected to address the agenda of finding a “permanent political solution” to the long-standing issues of Darjeeling hills within the ambit of constitutional framework, in lines with the BJP’s pre-poll promise for the affairs of Darjeeling hills. Besides Adhikari, also present at the meeting were Gorkha Janmukti Morcha (GJM) chief Bimal Gurung, and the party’s senior leader Roshan Giri, GNLF chief Mann Ghisingh, several state ministers and BJP MLAs from the hills, besides senior officials of the state government. Attempts made by previous state governments to address the issue through arrangements such as the establishment of the DGHC and the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (GTA) have, arguably, failed to secure long-term peace, economic prosperity and political stability in the region.

In October, 2025, the MHA appointed retired IPS officer and former deputy national security advisor Pankaj Kumar Singh as the official government interlocutor for the issue.
His role focuses on leading political dialogue and addressing long-standing demands of the Gorkha community.
Bista, the Darjeeling MP, said that Saturday’s meeting was held on a historic day since it coincided with the date of signing of the Gorkha accord in 1988.

The accord, signed between the Centre, the West Bengal government and the Gorkha National Liberation Front (GNLF), had led to the creation of the Darjeeling Gorkha Hill Council (DGHC) following a violent agitation for a separate state of Gorkhaland.
“The history of struggle of the hill communities spans over four decades during which the previous Left and TMC government trampled over the aspirations of the hill people.
The sacrifice made by our people involves nearly 2,000 people who were martyred, over 5,000 people displaced and women tortured and raped,” he alleged.

Bista said that while representatives of the various communities put forth their concerns and expectations at the meeting, Adhikari also spoke on how he intends to address the issues of the hill people.
“After hearing out all stakeholders, Shah summed up the meeting by elucidating how a permanent solution to the issue would be reached in the days ahead,” the MP said.

Besides Adhikari, also present at the meeting were Gorkha Janmukti Morcha (GJM) chief Bimal Gurung, and the party’s senior leader Roshan Giri, GNLF chief Mann Ghisingh, several state ministers and BJP MLAs from the hills, besides senior officials of the state government.

Attempts made by previous state governments to address the issue through arrangements such as the establishment of the DGHC and the Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (GTA) have, arguably, failed to secure long-term peace, economic prosperity and political stability in the region.

stories.headline: You are here because of someone’s blessings: Ruhullah to Nasir Aslam Wani
stories.title: You are here because of someone’s blessings: Ruhullah to Nasir Aslam Wani
stories.summary: Senior National Conference leader and Srinagar Member of Parliament Syed Aga Ruhullah Mehdi on Saturday hit back at Chief Minister Omar Abdullah’s adviser Nasir Aslam Wani, asserting that his political standing was backed by the trust and mandate of the people. Talking to reporters on the sidelines of a book launch ceremony here, Ruhullah was responding to Wani’s remarks questioning his position in the National Conference and suggesting that some leaders held positions because of the “blessings of a particular individual”. “Wherever I am today, it is because of the trust of people in me. Wherever you are, it is because of the blessings of a particular individual,” Ruhullah said. Earlier, Wani had told reporters that he was unaware of Ruhullah’s position in the party. “You people better visit Budgam and ask him. I cannot comment on him. I have not yet checked about his role in the party,” Wani said. “He (Ruhullah) can better explain if he is still in the party or not,” he added. Ruhullah further escalated his attack, claiming that elected MLAs were being “silenced” and were required to seek permission from someone who had himself lost an election by more than 10,000 votes. The remarks appeared to be a reference to Wani’s defeat in the 2024 Assembly elections from the Kupwara constituency, where Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) candidate Mir Mohammad Fayaz secured 27,773 votes against Wani’s 17,976, defeating him by 9,797 votes. Ruhullah, meanwhile, secured a decisive victory in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections from Srinagar, defeating PDP candidate Waheed Para by more than 1.88 lakh votes. Ruhullah polled 3.56 lakh votes, accounting for 52.8 per cent of the total votes, while Para secured 1.68 lakh votes, or 24.9 per cent. The exchange comes amid growing differences within the National Conference over the party’s political direction, with Ruhullah having publicly criticised the government and the party leadership on issues including reservation, restoration of constitutional rights and the electricity tariff hike. Ruhullah has also maintained that his political position is rooted in the mandate given to him by voters and that he intends to continue pursuing the issues on which he sought their support.
